title: The lilies of the field (Matthew 6:28–34)
hook: consider the lilies; don't worry about tomorrow, today has enough

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birds of the air: busy all day, and no barns full of worry. Your line was look at the birds. Did you find one? Day two hundred fifty-four.

Think about how much time goes into what we wear. The morning standing in front of the closet. The shirt that's fine but not quite right. The outfit for the interview, the wedding, the first date. Clothes say who we are, or who we're afraid we aren't. In Jesus's world, cloth was expensive. Most people owned very little of it, and a good coat could be the most valuable thing a family had. So when he moves from food to clothes, he's touching a real fear. And again he doesn't argue. He crouches down, so to speak, and points at the ground. Today, the lilies of the field.
screen: `THE MORNING AT THE CLOSET.` → `CLOTH WAS PRECIOUS.` → `HE POINTS AT THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." Consider is a careful word. The Greek means to learn something thoroughly, to study it until you understand. So this is homework: go and really look at a flower. Which flower? Nobody knows. The word is general, and many scholars think Jesus meant the wildflowers that cover Galilee's hills in spring, whatever grew at his feet that day. Then Solomon. He was the richest king in Israel's memory, and a wild flower outdresses him. And the next line is sharper: the grass is here today and tomorrow it's thrown in the oven. In a land short of wood, dried grass fueled the cooking fire. Beautiful and brief. If God dresses something that brief so lavishly, the reasoning goes, how much more you. Then he gives the order of things: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you." First. Not only. The food and clothes still matter; they just aren't the center. And he ends with one of the most honest lines in the Bible: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." It doesn't promise that today will be easy. It says today has enough trouble of its own. Don't borrow tomorrow's too. You only have to carry one day at a time.
screen: `CONSIDER: STUDY IT CLOSELY.` · `SOLOMON, OUTDRESSED.` · `SEEK YE FIRST.` · `SUFFICIENT UNTO THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: consider one flower. If you have one near you, a plant on the sill, a weed by the door, pick it up or lean in close. If not, picture one you know well. Look at the edges of the petals, the color where it changes, the center. Nobody sewed that. Let the next two minutes be only today. If tomorrow's list starts talking, tell it: tomorrow will take care of itself. The bell holds the time.
The lilies of the field. Wildflowers that outdress a king, here today, gone tomorrow, and dressed anyway.
screen: `THE LILIES OF THE FIELD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: today is enough. Tonight, when tomorrow's worries line up, name one of them, and say out loud: that's tomorrow's. Day two hundred fifty-four.

screen: `DAY 254 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SPECK AND THE PLANK.`

howItsDone: Many Christians read Matthew 6:34 in hard seasons and try to live one day at a time, and some keep a flower or a plant in view as a small reminder of the passage.

fork.setup: you're worried about what to wear and what to eat. Jesus doesn't say those don't matter. what does he say to do with them?
options: seek the kingdom first, and let these come after.

original.note: Greek: consider, learn thoroughly; from the verb for learning.

trapdoor: what you thought: stop caring about clothes and money.
what it means: seek God's kingdom first; carry one day at a time, because each day has enough of its own.
what a scholar hears: katamanthanō, a learning word; dried grass as oven fuel; and Solomon, the byword for glory, outshone by a weed.

notes: The identity of the 'lilies' (krina) is uncertain; the script says so and offers the common wildflower reading. Confirm.
Dried grass as oven fuel in a wood-poor land: common commentary note; confirm.
Cloth as costly in first-century Galilee: general social-history claim; confirm the wording.
